title: Bit Magic
html:
Bit manipulation treats an integer as a row of 0/1 switches. A handful of operators (& | ^ ~ << >>) and a dozen tricks turn O(n) counting problems into O(1) formulas, cancel paired elements with XOR, and enumerate every subset of a set with a counter.

Bit magic — solving problems by operating directly on the binary representation of integers — testing, setting, clearing and counting bits, and using XOR's cancelling property — instead of on their decimal value.

Binary representation and two's complement

An n-bit integer has n positions; bit 0 is the least significant bit (LSB, rightmost, worth 1) and bit n-1 the most significant bit (MSB, leftmost). Unsigned numbers use all bits for magnitude; signed numbers use two's complement, where the MSB acts as the sign and the representable range is -2^(n-1) … 2^(n-1) - 1.

1
Write the positive number
3 in 4 bits is 0011.
2
Invert every bit
0011 → 1100 (this is the one's complement).
3
Add 1
1100 + 1 → 1101. That is -3 in 4-bit two's complement.
two's complement of x in n bits = 2^n − x (4 bits: 16 − 3 = 13 = 1101)

Why two's complement rather than a separate sign bit? Three reasons that make hardware simpler:

  • One zero. A sign-magnitude scheme has +0 and -0; two's complement has a single 0000.
  • Addition just works. The same adder handles positive and negative operands: 3 + (-3) = 0011 + 1101 = 1 0000, and dropping the carry gives 0000. Subtraction is addition of the complement, which is where the name 0 − x comes from.
  • The leading bit is the sign. MSB 1 ⇒ negative, so a sign test is a single bit check.
Key point

Masking with (x >> i) & 1 works for negative numbers too, because every language above shifts a negative int arithmetically (the sign bit is copied in). Python has no fixed width, so -3 is conceptually …11111101 with infinitely many leading ones — taking the low 4 bits still gives 1101.

Bitwise operators

OperatorNameRule per bit12 (1100) with 10 (1010)
a & bAND1 only if both bits are 11000 = 8
a | bOR1 if either bit is 11110 = 14
a ^ bXOR1 if the bits differ0110 = 6
~aNOTflips every bit; equals -a - 1 in two's complement~12 = -13
a << kleft shiftshift left, zeros enter on the right; multiplies by 2^k12 << 2 = 48
a >> kright shiftshift right, drops the low bits; divides by 2^k (floor)12 >> 2 = 3

Language differences you must know

PythonC++ / JavaJavaScript
Width of an intunbounded — 1 << 100 is fine, ~x is always -x-132-bit int, 64-bit long/long long; overflow wraps (Java) or is undefined for signed (C++)numbers are doubles, but every bitwise operator converts to a 32-bit signed int first — 1 << 31 is -2147483648
>> on negativesarithmetic (floor division by 2^k)arithmetic; C++ guarantees it since C++20arithmetic
Logical (zero-fill) shiftnot needed — mask first: (x & 0xFFFFFFFF) >> kJava: x >>> k. C++: cast to unsigned firstx >>> k
Shift by ≥ widthfine (just a bigger number)undefined in C++, taken mod 32/64 in Javataken mod 32
Popcount built-inn.bit_count() (3.10+) or bin(n).count('1')std::popcount (<bit>, unsigned) / __builtin_popcount; Integer.bitCount(n)none — n.toString(2).split('1').length - 1
Pitfall

In JavaScript 2 ** 40 | 0 silently truncates to 32 bits, and in C++ 1 << 31 on an int and any shift by 32 or more are undefined behaviour. When you need 64 bits use 1n << 40n (BigInt) in JS and 1LL << 40 / 1L << 40 in C++/Java.

n | (1 << k)set bit kOR with the mask forces a 1

n ^ (1 << k)toggle bit kXOR with 1 flips, with 0 keeps
n & (n - 1)clear the rightmost set bitsubtracting 1 flips that bit and the zeros after it
n & -n (= n & ~(n - 1))isolate the rightmost set bit-n agrees with n only at that bit
n & (n - 1) == 0n is a power of two (for n > 0)a power of two has exactly one set bit

Decimal to binary and back

Repeated division by 2 produces the bits from the right: the remainder is the next bit, the quotient is what is left. Reading a binary string left to right is the reverse: value = value * 2 + bit. Both loops are O(number of bits) = O(log n).

Key point

The built-ins do the same: Python bin(37) / int('100101', 2), C++ bitset<8>(37) / stoi(s, nullptr, 2), Java Integer.toBinaryString(37) / Integer.parseInt(s, 2), JavaScript (37).toString(2) / parseInt(s, 2).

Check whether the kth bit is set

Example

Input: n = 5, k = 1
Output: Yes
Input: n = 5, k = 2
Output: No
Input: n = 5, k = 3
Output: Yes

Bits are counted from the right, so the kth bit (1-based) is the mask 1 << (k - 1); k must not exceed the width of n. Two equivalent ways:

Idea

Move the mask to the bit: n & (1 << (k-1)) keeps only bit k; the result is non-zero exactly when that bit is 1. Or move the bit to the mask: (n >> (k-1)) & 1 drags bit k down to position 0 and reads it as 0 or 1.

Time O(1)Space O(1)
Key point

Way 2 is the one to use when you want the bit's value (0/1) rather than a yes/no — e.g. when reading a number bit by bit. Both are a single AND plus a shift.

Pitfall

if n & (1 << (k-1)) == 1 is wrong for k > 1: the AND leaves the bit in place, so the result is 4 for k = 3, not 1. Compare with != 0 (or use the shift form). Also, in C++ 1 << 31 overflows a signed int — use 1u << k or 1LL << k for high bits.

Count set bits

Example

Input: n = 5
Output: 2
Input: n = 13
Output: 3
Input: n = 255
Output: 8

The number of 1 bits is also called the population count or Hamming weight. There are four standard ways, from obvious to fastest.

Naive: walk the bits from LSB to MSB — n % 2 (or n & 1) reads the lowest bit, n // 2 (or n >> 1) drops it. Runs once per bit, set or not.

Time O(number of bits) = O(log n)Space O(1)
Pitfall

With an arithmetic shift (>>) a negative n never reaches zero — -1 >> 1 is still -1 — so the loop runs forever. Use the logical shift (>>> in Java/JS, cast to unsigned in C++) or loop a fixed 32 times. Python's n >>= 1 on a negative number has the same problem.

Brian Kernighan's algorithm: n & (n - 1) clears the rightmost set bit, so the loop runs once per set bit instead of once per bit position. For a sparse number it is much faster.

Time O(number of set bits)Space O(1)

Lookup table: precompute the count for every byte value 0…255 once (O(1), it is a constant 256 entries), then a 32-bit number is just four table reads. Each entry is built from a smaller one: tbl[i] = (i & 1) + tbl[i >> 1].

Time O(1) — four lookupsSpace O(1) — a fixed 256-entry table

Built-ins: in production code use the library — it compiles to a single popcnt instruction where the CPU has one.

Is n a power of 2?

Example

Input: n = 4
Output: Yes
Input: n = 6
Output: No
Input: n = 0
Output: No

Naive: keep halving while n is even; it is a power of two if you end at exactly 1. O(log n).

Idea

A power of two has exactly one set bit (1, 10, 100, 1000…). n & (n - 1) clears the rightmost set bit, so for a power of two it leaves 0; any other positive number still has a bit left. n = 0 has no set bit at all and must be rejected separately — 0 & (0 - 1) is also 0.

Time O(1)Space O(1)
Pitfall

Two edge cases: n = 0 passes the n & (n-1) == 0 test but is not a power of two, and a negative n such as -2147483648 (INT_MIN, a single set bit in 32 bits) also passes. Write n > 0 && (n & (n - 1)) == 0 when negatives are possible.

Find the one odd-occurring element

Example

Input: arr = [10, 30, 30, 10, 30, 30, 20]
Output: 20
Input: arr = [4, 3, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5]
Output: 3

Every element appears an even number of times except one. Naive: for each element count its occurrences with a second loop and return the first with an odd count — O(n²).

Idea

XOR is commutative and associative, x ^ x = 0 and x ^ 0 = x. XOR-ing the whole array therefore lets every pair cancel itself regardless of order, and the only thing left standing is the element that had no partner.

Time O(n)Space O(1)
Key point

The same trick solves missing number (XOR 1…n with the array — the missing value survives) and find the element that appears once while the rest appear twice. It fails when more than one element is odd-occurring — the result is the XOR of all of them — which is exactly the next problem.

Find the two odd-occurring elements

Example

Input: arr = [3, 4, 3, 4, 5, 4, 4, 6, 7, 7]
Output: 5 6
Input: arr = [20, 15, 20, 16]
Output: 15 16

Now exactly two elements, x and y, occur an odd number of times. XOR-ing everything gives x ^ y, which is not enough on its own — we need to separate them.

Idea

x ^ y has a 1 exactly where x and y differ. Take its rightmost set bit, sn = xors & -xors. Partition the array into elements that have that bit set and elements that do not: x lands in one group and y in the other, and every paired element lands in the same group as its partner. XOR each group separately and the pairs cancel again, leaving x in one group and y in the other.

Time O(n)Space O(1)
Pitfall

The two results come out in group order, not sorted — which group holds the smaller value depends on the bit chosen. Sort the pair (as above) or the output will look random. xors & -xors relies on two's complement: -xors is ~xors + 1, which agrees with xors only at the rightmost set bit.

Power set using bitmasks

Example

Input: s = "abc"
Output: {} {a} {b} {a,b} {c} {a,c} {b,c} {a,b,c}

Idea

A set of n elements has 2^n subsets, and there are exactly 2^n integers from 0 to 2^n - 1. Read each counter as a mask: bit j set means include s[j]. Looping the counter enumerates every subset exactly once, with no recursion.

Time O(2^n · n)Space O(n) for the current subset
Key point

Bitmasks are the standard way to iterate over subsets in bitmask DP (travelling salesman, assignment problems): the mask is the state, mask | (1 << j) adds an element, mask & ~(1 << j) removes one, and __builtin_popcount(mask) tells how many are chosen. The recursive include/exclude version of this problem is in the Recursion topic.

Interview Q&A

Why does n & (n - 1) clear the rightmost set bit?

Subtracting 1 borrows from the rightmost 1: that bit becomes 0 and every 0 to its right becomes 1; the bits to its left are untouched. AND-ing with n keeps the untouched left part and zeroes everything from that bit rightwards. Example: 12 = 1100, 11 = 1011, 12 & 11 = 1000.

How do you check if two integers have opposite signs without comparing them?

(x ^ y) < 0. The sign bit of the XOR is 1 exactly when the sign bits differ. Related: x and y have the same parity iff ((x ^ y) & 1) == 0.

What is the difference between >> and >>>?

>> is an arithmetic shift: the sign bit is copied into the vacated positions, so -16 >> 2 = -4 (floor division). >>> (Java, JavaScript) is a logical shift that fills with zeros, so -16 >>> 2 is 1073741820 — the number reinterpreted as unsigned. C++ gets the logical behaviour by casting to unsigned; Python has unbounded ints, so mask to a width first.

Every element appears three times except one. Does XOR still work?

Plain XOR does not, because x ^ x ^ x = x — triples do not cancel. Count the set bits per position: each of the 32 positions has a count that is a multiple of 3 plus the lone element's bit, so count % 3 rebuilds the answer in O(32·n). Alternatively use two accumulators (ones, twos) that act as a mod-3 counter per bit.

How would you find the missing number in 1…n with one slot missing, without extra space?

XOR all numbers 1…n and XOR all array elements; everything present cancels and the missing number remains. The sum formula n(n+1)/2 − sum(arr) also works but can overflow a 32-bit int for large n, which XOR never does.

When is the lookup-table popcount actually better than Kernighan's loop?

When numbers are dense (many set bits) and you count millions of them: the table is a constant four array reads with no data-dependent branch, whereas Kernighan does one iteration per set bit (up to 32). For a few calls, or sparse numbers, the loop is simpler and just as fast. In real code use the built-in — it maps to the hardware popcnt instruction.
